name: Eyebrow growth serum

lead: Eyebrow growth serums are topical products, often containing peptides or botanical extracts, sold to make sparse brows look denser and fuller. Fuller brows frame the eyes and strengthen the upper face.

In looksmaxxing communities they are discussed alongside castor oil, microneedling, minoxidil and prescription prostaglandin analogues. Published work centres on prescription bimatoprost applied to brows, while a 2019 paper reported on a plant-derived extract (Jarilla-Coffea) described as improving eyelash and eyebrow growth in women. No trials of peptide serums for brows were found.

paras: The serum is applied to the brows, usually once or twice daily over a period of weeks to months. Users often combine it with castor oil, microneedling or minoxidil. Makers and forum users describe peptides as stimulating follicle activity.
Eye-area products can irritate. Bimatoprost, a prescription drug, has its own documented effects such as eyelid darkening, and findings from bimatoprost studies do not carry over to peptide serums.

angle.text: Users apply peptide or botanical serums to make sparse brows look denser and fuller, often alongside castor oil, microneedling or minoxidil. The idea is that the serum stimulates the brow follicles. Published work centres on prescription bimatoprost rather than over-the-counter products.

lead: Eyebrow growth serums are topical cosmetic products, often containing peptides or botanical extracts, marketed to make sparse brows look denser or fuller. They are discussed in looksmaxxing communities alongside castor oil, microneedling, minoxidil and prescription prostaglandin analogues.[1][2]

Published evidence specific to over-the-counter serums is thin. A 2019 paper in Clinical, Cosmetic and Investigational Dermatology reported on a plant-derived extract (Jarilla-Coffea) described as improving eyelash and eyebrow growth in women.[3] Studies of bimatoprost, a prescription prostaglandin analogue, have examined its use on eyebrows.[4][5]

paras: Serums are brushed or dabbed onto the brow area. Products vary widely, and some contain ingredients that forum users have catalogued from cosmetic-ingredient lists, such as myristoyl pentapeptide-17, myristoyl hexapeptide-16 and octapeptide-2, which supporters describe as stimulating hair-related keratin genes or counteracting inhibitory signals in follicles.

A 2011 report in Dermatologic Surgery examined bimatoprost ophthalmic solution 0.03% for eyebrow growth.[4] A 2020 retrospective study in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology followed 48 patients with eyebrow hypotrichosis treated with bimatoprost 0.01% over 24 weeks, analysing changes in hair density and diameter by part of the brow (head, body, tail).[5] These concern a prescription drug rather than over-the-counter serums.

The 2019 Jarilla-Coffea extract paper, whose title reports improved lash and brow growth in women, is the main published study identified of a cosmetic botanical product.[3] No trial of peptide-based brow serums was found.

A looksmax.org thread lists peptide ingredients and asks members to find a serum containing them; a reply asks for a breakdown of how legitimate each is, and the original poster says they are legitimate but a good product is hard to find. Another thread asks about the best microneedling approach for brow growth. Castor oil is also recommended in forum answers, with one user saying shaved brows return within two to four weeks.

lore.intro: Brow-growth products are discussed as part of 'eyebrowmaxxing', often as a stack with other treatments.

claims.claim: Specific peptides can stimulate brow hair growth

timeline.event: Report on bimatoprost 0.03% for eyebrow growth published.[4]
